source_review.notes: Checked the ARIES primary paper, Gray and Reuter, current PostgreSQL 18 checkpoint/WAL documentation and implementation surface, MySQL 8.4 InnoDB checkpoint/redo documentation, and current SQLite WAL format and checkpoint documentation through publisher or official records.

evidence: Defined begin/end checkpoint LSNs, checkpoint pointer, DPT, recLSN, pageLSN, redo horizon, dirty generations, checkpoint age, and recovery oracle before use.
Checked minimum-frontier, page-version, log coverage, time/byte age, and durability terminology for distinct meanings.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Checkpoint location, redo start, transaction outcome, page cleanliness, and log-retention ownership remain distinct typed concepts.

evidence: Recomputed initial redo horizon min(140,220,340)=140, post-P-flush horizon min(220,340)=220, and combined retention frontier min(220,260,120,500,200)=120.
Recomputed Exercise 2 initial horizon 90 and, under the stated generation assumptions, final DPT {B:330,C:240} with horizon 240.
numerical_recomputation.notes: All example frontiers were recomputed independently; segment rounding is deliberately left engine-specific.

evidence: Reviewed R=min recLSN(D) under the premise that D contains every page whose logged effect may be absent and each recLSN is conservative.
Reviewed the recycle-frontier inequality over crash redo, rollback, replica, archive, backup, and decoder obligations.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The horizon conclusion is conditional on complete DPT coverage; false negatives invalidate the bound.

evidence: Reviewed empty DPT, horizon older than checkpoint begin, redirty during in-flight write, transaction outcome during capture, incomplete payload, torn pointer, corrupt checksum, stale incarnation, and restartpoint boundaries.

Reviewed storage full, huge dirty/transaction tables, long losers, stalled consumers, write reordering, full-page amplification, unknown formats, repeated recovery crashes, and silent index corruption.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Ambiguous persistence or metadata integrity fails closed or falls back to an older validated checkpoint.

evidence: Checked capture coverage, first-dirty recLSN retention, compare-and-clear generation matching, payload-before-pointer publication, WAL-before-page persistence, and minimum-owner retention.
The executable fixture reconstructed discovery, redo, DPT advancement, active-transaction, empty-DPT, and recycle-frontier states.
invariant_checking.notes: Conservative extras can increase work; unsafe omissions or prematurely advanced frontiers are rejected.

evidence: Reviewed the horizon-safety argument and confirmed that its DPT completeness and conservative recLSN premises are explicitly stated.
Reviewed crash cuts around checkpoint payload flush and pointer publication, plus the redirty compare-and-clear argument.
proof_review.notes: The chapter does not claim that a bounded scan proves bounded recovery time or state correctness.

evidence: Audited safe, complete, durable, current, exact, conservative, bounded, atomic, checkpoint, restartpoint, recovery, and retained language.
Separated general checkpoint models from product-specific PostgreSQL, InnoDB, and SQLite behavior.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: All guarantees are scoped to declared recovery, persistence, format, incarnation, and consumer assumptions.

evidence: The CPython 3.14.4 fixture reproduced the finite checkpoint-horizon and retention calculations on macOS 13.7.8 x86_64.
Independent calculations reproduced the compact example, executable fixture, and exercise frontier values.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The fixture validates finite decision arithmetic only; it does not emulate concurrency, persistence, corruption, or full database recovery.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed checkpoint purpose, quiescent/fuzzy models, DPT and transaction capture, redo-horizon derivation, publication, WAL ordering, cleaning, retention, scheduling, full-page protection, restartpoints, and validation.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed redirty races, torn and stale metadata, storage ordering, resource reserves, long transactions, replicas/backups/decoders, checkpoint latency cliffs, format compatibility, canary telemetry, incident evidence, and rollback.

pedagogical_review.notes: The Level-II chapter derives checkpoints from recovery obligations, connects formal frontiers to production behavior, supplies one executable model, ten distinct worked examples, and five progressive exercises with complete answers.

limitations: Internal source, mathematical, snippet, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical review only; no external academic, database-vendor, storage-vendor, standards, security, operations, or production review is claimed. Conclusions remain conditional on recovery algorithm, DPT and transaction-table completeness, record/page formats, log history and database incarnation, memory ordering, WAL and device persistence semantics, page identity and integrity, transaction outcomes, retention owners, workload, resources, configuration, implementation, and future version drift.
